items.text: A restoration company signs a GC's standard subcontract. It has a merger clause stating the writing is the entire agreement. The GC's project manager had verbally promised, before signing, that the company would be paid time-and-materials for any hidden mold found, but the signed contract is silent on mold pricing and only states a flat scope price. Mold turns up. Under UAW-GM Human Resource Center v KSL Recreation Corp, can the company enforce the verbal time-and-materials promise?

C. No, not unless the company can show fraud relating to the merger clause itself, or fraud invalidating the entire contract including the merger clause — UAW-GM v KSL holds a valid merger clause is conclusive proof of integration and nullifies prior agreements; the only fraud that survives it is fraud about the merger clause itself or fraud invalidating the whole contract.
What is the correct Michigan Court of Appeals citation and decision date for UAW-GM Human Resource Center v KSL Recreation Corp?
B. 228 Mich App 486, decided March 6, 1998 — The confirmed citation, opened this run, is 228 Mich App 486 (1998), decided by the Michigan Court of Appeals on March 6, 1998, published.

A commercial property owner's lease requires the tenant to "indemnify, defend, and hold harmless" the owner for any claim arising from the tenant's negligence. A customer is injured in the tenant's leased space and sues the owner. No one has yet determined whether the tenant was actually negligent. What is the practical significance of treating "indemnify" and "defend" as separate obligations here?

A. The defend obligation can require the tenant to fund or provide the owner's legal defense while the lawsuit is still pending, before fault is ever decided, separately from the later indemnify question of who pays a judgment — Indemnify and defend are distinct, separable duties that can be owed on different timelines. The duty to defend has been described by Michigan courts, in the insurance-duty context, as broader than and triggered independently of the duty to indemnify.

American Bumper & Mfg Co v Hartford Fire Ins Co and Auto-Owners Ins Co v City of Clare both hold that the duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify. In what specific legal context did Michigan's Supreme Court establish that rule?

D. An insurer's duty to defend its own policyholder under an insurance policy — Both cases are insurance-duty cases describing an insurer's duty to defend its policyholder. Applying that identical rule to a non-insurance commercial indemnity clause is practitioner logic, not a cited Michigan holding verified this run.

A water-mitigation equipment rental contract caps the rental company's total liability at the amount of the rental fee paid, for any damage the equipment causes. The equipment fails due to an ordinary manufacturing defect that neither party knew about, causing water damage to the customer's property. Under Xu v Gay and general limitation-of-liability doctrine, does the cap likely apply?

A. Yes, because this is ordinary negligence at most, not gross negligence or willful misconduct, so the cap is not barred by Xu v Gay's line — Xu v Gay bars waiving liability for gross negligence or willful and wanton misconduct, defined as conduct so reckless as to demonstrate a substantial lack of concern for whether injury results. An unknown manufacturing defect is ordinary-negligence territory at most, so a properly drafted cap should apply.

A supply agreement for restoration materials states that the buyer's exclusive remedy for defective goods is repair or replacement by the seller. After three failed repair attempts, the goods still do not work and the buyer has lost significant business income waiting on them. Under MCL 440.2719(2), what happens to the buyer's remedies?

B. Because the exclusive remedy has failed of its essential purpose, the buyer may pursue remedy as otherwise provided under the UCC — MCL 440.2719(2) provides that where circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to fail of its essential purpose, remedy may be had as provided in the act, reopening ordinary UCC remedies.

A commercial contract for drying equipment limits the seller's liability for consequential damages (like lost business income from a delayed dry-out) arising from a defective unit. The buyer is a commercial restoration company, not a consumer. Under MCL 440.2719(3), is that limitation presumptively unconscionable?

A. No, the presumption of unconscionability under the statute applies to limiting consequential damages for personal injury in consumer goods cases, not to commercial-loss limitations — MCL 440.2719(3) makes a limitation of consequential damages for personal injury in consumer goods cases prima facie unconscionable, but expressly says a limitation where the loss is commercial is not treated that way.

A homeowner's purchase agreement for a fire-damaged property states, "This Agreement is subject to Buyer obtaining financing approval on or before 30 days from signing." Financing is never approved. Under the condition-precedent framework from Harbor Park Market, Inc v Gronda, does the seller have a breach claim against the buyer for failing to close?

A. Likely no, if the financing-approval language is a condition precedent: the triggering event never happened, so there may have been no right to performance, and thus no breach, in the first place — Harbor Park Market defines a condition precedent as a fact or event that must occur before there is a right to performance. If financing approval is drafted as a condition precedent and never happens, the obligation to close may never have arisen, so there is no breach to sue on.
According to Harbor Park Market, Inc v Gronda, 277 Mich App 126 (2007), how inclined are Michigan courts to read an ambiguous contract stipulation as a condition precedent rather than a covenant?

C. Michigan courts are not inclined to construe stipulations as conditions precedent unless the contract's clear language compels that reading — Harbor Park Market states courts are "not inclined to construe stipulations of a contract as conditions precedent" absent clear language compelling that result; the court's actual holding rested on this specific clause's wording, not a blanket rule.

A roofing contract signed in June, with no "time is of the essence" clause, sets a completion date of August 1. The contractor finishes August 6 because a shingle shipment was delayed by the manufacturer. Under MacRitchie v Plumb, 70 Mich App 242 (1976), is the five-day delay ordinarily treated as a material breach that lets the homeowner terminate the whole contract?

B. No, because time is not regarded as of the essence of a contract unless made so by express provision, the nature of the contract, or the circumstances of its execution, none of which are described here — MacRitchie v Plumb sets the default that time is not of the essence absent an express provision, the nature of the contract, or the circumstances of execution making it so. A short delay without a time-is-of-the-essence clause is ordinarily a minor breach, not grounds for termination.

Same roofing contract as above, but this time it explicitly states, "Time is of the essence; Contractor shall complete all work by August 1." The contractor finishes August 6. How does adding that clause change the legal analysis of the same five-day delay?

D. It flips the default, so the five-day delay can be treated as a material breach allowing the homeowner to terminate the contract, not merely collect delay damages — MacRitchie v Plumb's default (time not essential absent express provision) is flipped once the parties expressly make time essential; a missed deadline can then be treated as a material breach rather than a minor one.
What is Michigan's "American Rule" on attorney fees, as stated in Great Lakes Shores, Inc v Bartley, 311 Mich App 252 (2015)?

A. Attorney fees are not recoverable from a losing party unless authorized by a statute, court rule, or other recognized exception, such as a contractual fee-shifting clause — Great Lakes Shores v Bartley states the American Rule and confirms a contractual fee-shifting clause between the parties is a recognized, enforceable exception to it.

A restoration company joins a referral network under a vendor agreement that says, "Contractor shall pay Network's reasonable attorney fees incurred in any dispute arising from this Agreement," with no language about Network paying the contractor's fees. What kind of fee-shifting clause is this, and why does the direction matter?

B. A one-way clause that only ever exposes the contractor to the Network's legal bill, regardless of who actually wins the dispute, which changes who can afford to fight a disputed claim — This is a one-way fee-shifting clause: it exposes only the contractor to the other side's fees, with no reciprocal right, unlike a mutual "prevailing party" clause that cuts both ways.

A vendor contract requires any lawsuit to be filed only in a named court in another state. The Michigan party sues in Michigan anyway. Under MCL 600.745(3), which of the following is NOT one of the statute's listed exceptions that would let the Michigan court keep the case?

A. The plaintiff simply prefers Michigan courts and its lawyer is located there — MCL 600.745(3) lists five specific exceptions (statutory mandate, inability to get effective relief elsewhere, substantial inconvenience of the other state, misrepresentation/duress/unconscionability, or general unfairness). Mere preference for Michigan or lawyer location is not one of them.
What did Turcheck v Amerifund Financial, Inc, 272 Mich App 341 (2006), say about Michigan's general policy toward contractual forum-selection clauses?

A. Michigan courts generally enforce contractual forum-selection clauses as written, and Michigan's public policy favors their enforcement, absent one of the statutory exceptions applying — Turcheck states Michigan courts generally enforce contractual forum-selection clauses under MCL 600.745(3), that Michigan's public policy favors their enforcement, and that absent a statutory exception, the clause is enforced as written.

A commercial property owner's work-order form includes both an out-of-state forum-selection clause and a jury-trial-waiver clause in the same paragraph. A small restoration company signs it without reading closely. What is the combined practical effect if a change-order dispute later goes to litigation?

A. The company has agreed in advance to litigate out of state before a judge alone, a combination that can make a modest dispute too expensive to pursue at all — Combining a forum-selection clause that Michigan courts generally enforce (Turcheck; MCL 600.745(3)) with a jury-trial waiver raises both the cost (travel, out-of-state counsel) and the stakes (no jury) of any future dispute, which is the practical point of pairing the two clauses.

Is the Michigan Court of Appeals decision commonly cited in practice for enforcing contractual jury-trial waivers, Andy J Egan Co v Pro Services, Inc (2018), relied on as a verified primary source anywhere in this domain?

B. No, the opinion could not be located and opened at a confirmed URL this run, so its content is flagged as unverified and should not be quoted or cited by name without opening it first — This domain flags Andy J Egan Co v Pro Services, Inc as [INSUFFICIENT_DATA]: it is widely reported in secondary Michigan practice commentary, but the opinion itself was not successfully opened this run, so its holding should not be cited or quoted as verified.

A mitigation-services scope-of-work section reads, "Price includes labor, materials, and equipment rental." A dispute arises over whether dumpster fees, not listed, are part of the price. As a general drafting canon (not a Michigan-specific holding verified this run), how does the non-exhaustive reading of "includes" affect this dispute?

C. It does not automatically resolve the dispute either way; because "includes" is read as illustrative rather than exhaustive by default, dumpster fees could be read as included even though unlisted, which can cut for either side depending on context — "Including" is non-exhaustive by default, which means an unlisted item is not automatically excluded, but that same default does not automatically include it either; it depends on context, which is exactly why the canon alone does not resolve a real dispute and careful drafting of a closed list matters more.

A work-authorization form mixes drafting signals: "Contractor shall begin work within 24 hours... Homeowner may cancel within 3 business days... Contractor will submit a final invoice within 10 days." Drawing on Manuel v Gill, 481 Mich 637 (2008) and general drafting practice, what should a careful reader flag about the word "will" in the third clause?

D. "Will" is grammatically a statement about the future rather than an obligation, so its appearance alongside "shall" (mandatory) and "may" (permissive) should prompt a question about whether the drafter actually meant a mandatory duty — Manuel v Gill confirms the general shall (mandatory) / may (permissive) default, though it construes a statute rather than a private contract. "Will" is a separate, general drafting signal (a statement about the future), and mixing it with shall and may in similar clauses invites ambiguity about what the drafter intended; no Michigan contract case on "will" specifically was opened this run.

A GC subcontract says the sub "shall hold harmless" the GC for property damage caused by the sub's crew, but says nothing separately about "indemnify" or "defend." How is "hold harmless" generally treated relative to "indemnify" in contract drafting, per general commentary (not a Michigan-specific holding verified this run)?

A. As functionally the same obligation: a promise not to pursue the other party for the loss, generally treated as equivalent to indemnify, distinct from the separate "defend" obligation (which this clause does not independently create) — General commentary treats "hold harmless" as functionally equivalent to "indemnify" (not pursuing the other party for the loss), distinct from "defend," which is a separate obligation to fund or provide a defense while a claim is pending; a clause using only "hold harmless" does not, by itself, create that separate defend duty.
